subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which equation correctly defines density?
questions.explain: Density is defined as the mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m ÷ V.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.explain: In SI units density is kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), from kilograms divided by cubic metres.

questions.q: Why is a solid usually much denser than the same substance as a gas?
options: Its particles are packed close together, so more mass fits in a given volume
Its particles are heavier when solid
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are closely packed, giving much more mass per unit volume than the widely spaced particles of a gas.

questions.q: A metal block has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 30 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explain: density = mass ÷ volume = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 g/cm³.

questions.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid according to the particle model?
options: In a regular, closely packed arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions
Randomly spaced and moving quickly in all directions
Close together but able to flow past one another
Far apart with no forces between them
questions.explain: Solid particles are held in a fixed, regular pattern by strong forces and can only vibrate in place.

questions.q: Why can a gas be compressed much more easily than a liquid?
options: There are large spaces between the gas particles
Gas particles are smaller than liquid particles
Gas particles attract each other strongly
Gas particles are arranged in a regular pattern
questions.explain: Gas particles are widely spaced, so the gas can be squashed into a smaller volume, unlike a liquid whose particles are already close together.

questions.q: Why is a change of state described as a physical change rather than a chemical change?
options: The substance keeps the same chemical composition and the change can be reversed
A new substance with different properties is formed
The mass of the substance decreases
The particles are destroyed and recreated
questions.explain: In a change of state no new substance is made; the same particles are simply rearranged, so it is reversible.

questions.q: What name is given to a liquid turning into a gas from its surface at temperatures below its boiling point?
questions.explain: Evaporation is the change from liquid to gas that occurs at the surface of a liquid below its boiling point.

questions.q: While a pure solid is melting, its temperature stays constant even though it is still being heated. Why?
options: The energy supplied is used to break the bonds between particles rather than raise the temperature
The thermometer stops working during melting
The solid stops absorbing energy once it starts to melt
The particles lose kinetic energy as they melt
questions.explain: During melting the supplied energy increases the potential energy of the particles by breaking bonds, so temperature does not rise.

questions.q: The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance between which two states, at constant temperature?
questions.explain: Latent heat of fusion refers to melting/freezing, the change between solid and liquid at constant temperature.

questions.q: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 340 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 0.2 kg of ice at 0 °C?
Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid. What is this process called?
questions.explain: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.

questions.q: Which equation gives the energy needed to change the temperature of a substance?
options: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature
change in thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat
change in thermal energy = mass ÷ volume
change in thermal energy = mass × gravitational field strength × height
questions.explain: ΔE = m c Δθ links energy to mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 0.5 kg of water by 20 °C? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg°C)
What causes a gas to exert pressure on the walls of its container?
options: Gas particles colliding with the walls and exerting a force on them
Gas particles sticking to the walls
The weight of the gas pressing downwards only
Attraction between the walls and the particles
questions.explain: Gas pressure results from the many collisions of fast-moving particles with the container walls, each exerting a small force.

questions.q: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. Why does the gas pressure increase?
options: The particles move faster, hitting the walls harder and more often
The particles get bigger as they warm up
questions.explain: Raising the temperature increases the particles' average kinetic energy, so collisions with the walls become more frequent and more forceful, increasing pressure.

questions.q: How does the pressure in a liquid change as you go deeper below the surface?
options: It stays the same at all depths
questions.explain: The pressure in a liquid increases with depth because a greater weight of liquid acts above each point.

questions.q: Which equation gives the pressure due to a column of liquid?
options: pressure = height × density × gravitational field strength
questions.explain: For a liquid column, p = h ρ g, so pressure depends on depth, liquid density and gravitational field strength.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has a pressure of 200 kPa and a volume of 1.5 m³. It is compressed to 0.5 m³. What is the new pressure?
questions.explain: At constant temperature pV is constant, so p₂ = (200 × 1.5) ÷ 0.5 = 600 kPa.

questions.q: What happens to the total mass of a substance when it changes state, for example when ice melts to water?
options: The mass stays the same because mass is conserved
questions.explain: A change of state only rearranges the same particles, so the total mass is conserved.
